subtopic_detail: First UTI imaging in a child under 24 months per RCH CPG
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar reviewing an 18 month old girl in the short stay ward. She was admitted 48 hours ago with a first febrile urinary tract infection, culture positive for Escherichia coli sensitive to trimethoprim, and switched from IV to oral trimethoprim after 24 hours with rapid resolution of fever. Antenatal ultrasounds through the pregnancy were reported as normal with normal kidneys and bladder documented on the 20 week morphology scan. There is no family history of vesicoureteric reflux, no history of poor urinary stream, no palpable abdominal mass and she is now feeding, playing and afebrile for 36 hours.

Her mother works in a rural community two hours from the tertiary centre and asks what imaging her daughter needs before discharge to prevent kidney damage.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 118 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert, playing, abdomen soft, no flank fullness, no back or spinal abnormalities, external genitalia normal
data_table.Investigations: Urine culture Escherichia coli >10^8 CFU/mL sensitive to trimethoprim, creatinine 28 micromol/L, C reactive protein 42 mg/L falling from 96, blood culture negative

lead_in: What is the most appropriate imaging plan?

options.text: No routine renal tract imaging, provide safety net advice about recurrent fever with prompt urine collection
options.rationale: For a first typical urinary tract infection in a child aged 6 to 24 months who responds to antibiotics within 48 hours, has documented normal antenatal kidney imaging and no risk features for atypical infection, RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound; safety netting for recurrence is the appropriate plan. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound during this admission before discharge, with paediatric outpatient follow up
options.rationale: Ultrasound during illness is reserved for atypical urinary tract infection: poor response after 48 hours of antibiotics, non-Escherichia coli organism, sepsis, abdominal or bladder mass, or raised creatinine. None of those apply here. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Dimercaptosuccinic acid renal cortical scan in 4 to 6 months to assess for renal cortical scarring
options.rationale: The dimercaptosuccinic acid renal cortical scan is a NICE pathway construct, not part of the RCH imaging cascade. RCH does not use routine dimercaptosuccinic acid to assess scarring in a typical first infection. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Micturating cystourethrogram to exclude vesicoureteric reflux prior to discharge home to a rural community
options.rationale: Micturating cystourethrogram is invasive, carries a radiation and infection risk, and is not part of the RCH cascade after a first typical urinary tract infection in this age group. Reserve for recurrent infection or a hydronephrotic kidney on ultrasound. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

options.text: Renal tract ultrasound plus prophylactic trimethoprim for 6 months to prevent culture proven recurrence
options.rationale: Long term antibiotic prophylaxis is not recommended after a first typical infection in a child of this age without demonstrated high grade vesicoureteric reflux or an abnormal urinary tract. (Source: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection)

explanation.summary: In a child aged 6 to 24 months who has a first typical urinary tract infection with rapid clinical response and documented normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH does not recommend routine renal ultrasound, dimercaptosuccinic acid or micturating cystourethrogram. Ultrasound during the acute illness is reserved for features of atypical infection, and the dimercaptosuccinic acid and micturating cystourethrogram cascade is NICE, not RCH. Safety netting for recurrent fever and prompt clean catch urine at re-presentation is the appropriate plan. Documented antenatal monitoring and prompt clinical response together carry weight.
key_points: Atypical urinary tract infection triggers ultrasound during illness: poor response at 48 hours, non-Escherichia coli, sepsis, abdominal mass, raised creatinine.
Dimercaptosuccinic acid and micturating cystourethrogram are NOT in the RCH cascade after a first typical infection.
Antibiotic prophylaxis is reserved for demonstrated high grade vesicoureteric reflux or recurrence, not routine first infection.
explanation.pearls: For an 18 month old girl with a first Escherichia coli urinary tract infection that responds within 48 hours and normal antenatal renal imaging, RCH advises safety net advice with no routine imaging.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Urinary tract infection
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Paediatric urinary tract infection

subtopic_detail: Bronchiolitis oxygen escalation per RCH CPG
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a district general emergency department. A 7 month old previously well infant presents with 3 days of coryza, cough and rising work of breathing. His mother reports poor feeding for the last 12 hours and no wet nappy for 4 hours. He has no cyanosis at rest and is not sleepy. On examination he has bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, moderate subcostal recession and tracheal tug. There is no focal consolidation on auscultation.

His nasopharyngeal aspirate later confirms respiratory syncytial virus. He is nursed sitting up in a cot. A junior colleague has already commenced high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.4 within the first 10 minutes of arrival citing severity and pulls you aside asking whether that is correct first line oxygen.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 62 /min, SpO2 87% on room air, temperature 37.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Bilateral fine crackles and expiratory wheeze, subcostal recession, tracheal tug, capillary refill 2 s
data_table.Investigations: Nasopharyngeal aspirate later positive for respiratory syncytial virus; capillary blood gas pH 7.34 pCO2 46 mmHg lactate 1.4 mmol/L; chest X ray not performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial oxygen therapy?

options.text: Continue high flow nasal cannula at 2 L/kg/min with fraction of inspired oxygen 0.4 as commenced
options.rationale: High flow is reserved for infants who fail low flow after 2 hours; starting straight on high flow is not the RCH first line and can commit an infant to a higher acuity area unnecessarily. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Low flow nasal prong oxygen titrated to SpO2 target 90%, review at 60 minutes
options.rationale: First line oxygen for bronchiolitis is low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, titrated to SpO2 target 90% (not 92 to 94%); escalation to high flow is considered if low flow fails after 2 hours. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised salbutamol 2.5 mg back to back with review of oxygen needs after the third dose
options.rationale: Nebulised bronchodilators are not routinely recommended in bronchiolitis under 12 months and delay appropriate oxygen and feeding assessment. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Nebulised hypertonic saline 3 percent every 4 hours to reduce airway oedema
options.rationale: Hypertonic saline is not part of the RCH bronchiolitis pathway and has no reliable short stay benefit; it does not address the immediate hypoxia. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

options.text: Endotracheal intubation and mechanical ventilation because of respiratory rate above 60
options.rationale: Isolated tachypnoea in an infant who is not exhausted, apnoeic or unresponsive is not an indication for intubation; escalate through low flow then high flow first. (Source: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis)

explanation.summary: RCH recommends low flow nasal prong oxygen 1 to 2 L/min titrated to an SpO2 target of 90% as the first line for hypoxic bronchiolitis, with review at 60 to 120 minutes. High flow is not the first line and is reserved for children who deteriorate or do not improve on low flow after 2 hours. Salbutamol, hypertonic saline and steroids are not routinely recommended under 12 months. Oxygen is the primary supportive treatment; hydration by nasogastric or intravenous route is added as feeding deteriorates.
key_points: First line oxygen in bronchiolitis is nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min, target SpO2 90% under RCH.
High flow nasal cannula is a rescue after failure of low flow at 2 hours, not the initial setting.
Bronchodilators, hypertonic saline and steroids are not routinely used in bronchiolitis under 12 months.
explanation.pearls: For a 7 month old with respiratory syncytial virus bronchiolitis and SpO2 87%, start low flow nasal prong 1 to 2 L/min to a target 90%; do not open with high flow.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bronchiolitis
PREDICT Australasian Bronchiolitis Guideline 2024

subtopic_detail: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis fluid regimen and cerebral oedema risk
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar admitting a 9 year old boy with new onset type 1 diabetes and diabetic ketoacidosis. He has 2 weeks of polydipsia, polyuria and weight loss. He was Kussmaul breathing on arrival and drowsy but rousable, and the intensive care unit consultant has reviewed him and agrees he does not need immediate airway support. He has had one 10 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline bolus given over 30 minutes because of prolonged capillary refill and now looks better perfused.

His weight is 28 kg. You are asked to write the ongoing fluid and insulin plan. The retrieval team wants clear numbers so they can hand over to the paediatric intensive care unit at the tertiary centre in 90 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 128 /min, blood pressure 108/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 /min, SpO2 100% on room air, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable, Kussmaul breathing, capillary refill 2 s post bolus, moderate dehydration estimated at 7 percent
data_table.Investigations: Venous pH 7.05, HCO3 6 mmol/L, glucose 34 mmol/L, ketones 5.4 mmol/L, sodium 136 mmol/L, corrected sodium 143 mmol/L, potassium 4.6 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L

lead_in: Which fluid and insulin plan best matches AU paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis guidance?

options.text: 0.9 percent saline plus 20 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance plus 7 percent deficit replaced evenly over 48 hours, insulin 0.1 units/kg/hour starting 1 hour after fluids
options.rationale: The maintenance plus deficit approach is right but the deficit is capped at 5 to 7 percent regardless of clinical estimate and must be replaced over 48 hours using isotonic fluid with potassium; insulin should be at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour and started at least 1 hour after fluids. Adding 20 mmol/L potassium is only appropriate once serum potassium is known to be <5.5 mmol/L and urine output confirmed; the letter is close but the description misses the potassium detail and the insulin dose caveat that is separately assessed in option C. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: Two further 20 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline boluses back to back to correct dehydration rapidly, then commence insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately
options.rationale: Aggressive fluid boluses beyond an initial 10 mL/kg (repeated only for persistent shock) increase the risk of cerebral oedema. Insulin should not be started immediately as it worsens fluid shifts and cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.9 percent saline plus 40 mmol/L potassium chloride at maintenance plus 5 to 7 percent deficit over 48 hours, insulin infusion 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour starting 1 hour after fluids
options.rationale: RCH and ISPAD advise capped deficit of 5 to 7 percent regardless of estimate, replaced over 48 hours using isotonic fluid with 40 mmol/L potassium once serum potassium is <5.5 mmol/L and urine output established, insulin at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour started 1 hour after fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.45 percent saline with 5 percent dextrose at maintenance plus deficit over 24 hours, insulin infusion 0.1 units/kg/hour immediately at commencement of the fluid
options.rationale: Half normal saline as initial fluid and replacement over 24 hours are associated with rapid corrected sodium change and higher risk of cerebral oedema; RCH uses isotonic fluid, spread rehydration over 48 hours, and adds dextrose only once blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

options.text: 0.9 percent saline at 2 times maintenance for the first 4 hours to accelerate perfusion, insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour started with the fluids
options.rationale: Running fluids at 2 times maintenance during initial rehydration exceeds RCH capped rates, increases the risk of cerebral oedema, and starting insulin simultaneously worsens osmotic shift. (Source: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis)

explanation.summary: Paediatric diabetic ketoacidosis fluid management uses an initial 10 mL/kg isotonic bolus only if perfusion demands, then maintenance plus a capped 5 to 7 percent deficit spread evenly over 48 hours with isotonic fluid containing 40 mmol/L potassium once serum potassium is under 5.5 mmol/L and urine output is established. Insulin runs at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour, started at least 1 hour after fluids to reduce cerebral oedema risk. Dextrose is added when blood glucose falls below 15 mmol/L rather than dropping the insulin rate first. The disconfirming feature that kills the more aggressive options is the drowsy state on presentation, which raises baseline cerebral oedema risk.
key_points: Deficit is capped at 5 to 7 percent and replaced over 48 hours to minimise cerebral oedema.
Insulin starts 1 hour after fluids at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour.
Add dextrose when blood glucose falls under 15 mmol/L; do not reduce insulin first.
explanation.pearls: For a 28 kg child with pH 7.05, use isotonic fluid at maintenance plus 5 to 7 percent deficit over 48 hours, potassium 40 mmol/L once safe, insulin 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/hour started 1 hour later.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Diabetic ketoacidosis
ISPAD Clinical Practice Consensus 2022: DKA and hyperglycaemic hyperosmolar state

stem:
You are the paediatric emergency registrar on a Saturday overnight shift. A 6 week old male infant is brought in by his parents with 6 hours of fever and reduced feeding. He was a term uneventful spontaneous vaginal delivery, breastfeeding well, no birth complications, no maternal group B streptococcus positive swab, no prolonged rupture of membranes. He is now taking half his usual feed volume, mildly less alert than baseline but consolable and pink. There is no rash. There is no localising source of infection on examination.

He has had a full septic screen commenced including blood culture and urine sample. Point of care viral swab is negative so far. The parents ask whether the lumbar puncture the senior nurse mentioned is really needed since he is now smiling briefly at his mother. Your consultant says to follow the RCH pathway strictly for this age.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 82/48 mmHg, respiratory rate 46 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 38.4 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert but slightly quiet, anterior fontanelle soft, no rash, chest clear, abdomen soft, no focal source
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 6.2 x10^9/L, C reactive protein 18 mg/L, urine dip negative for nitrites and leukocytes, chest X ray clear

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management step next?

options.text: Discharge home with paracetamol as needed, safety net advice, return to review if fever persists at 24 to 48 hours
options.rationale: Any infant under 3 months with a temperature >=38.0 degC requires a full septic screen and empirical antibiotics; discharge without treatment carries an unacceptable meningitis and bacteraemia miss rate. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Empirical oral amoxicillin, admit for period of observation, defer lumbar puncture unless he clinically deteriorates
options.rationale: Oral antibiotics do not achieve reliable central nervous system penetration for bacterial meningitis and deferring lumbar puncture undertreats a serious bacterial infection risk in a 6 week old. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Empirical intravenous cefotaxime alone, defer lumbar puncture unless C reactive protein rises above 40 mg/L
options.rationale: C reactive protein trends do not exclude bacterial meningitis in this age group; deferring the lumbar puncture to observe biomarkers is not the RCH pathway for an under 3 month old with fever. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Lumbar puncture now, empirical intravenous cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus aciclovir, admit for period of observation
options.rationale: For any infant under 3 months with fever, RCH advises full septic screen including a lumbar puncture where safe, followed by empirical IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin (Listeria cover under 1 month; broadly used to under 2 to 3 months in some pathways) plus IV aciclovir until herpes simplex is excluded. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Nasal high flow oxygen plus intravenous saline bolus 20 mL/kg then transfer for further paediatric intensive care review
options.rationale: The child is not shocked or hypoxic and does not need high flow or a fluid bolus; the immediate priority is the septic screen and empirical antibiotics, not paediatric intensive care unit transfer. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

explanation.summary: A 6 week old with fever >=38.0 degC needs a full septic screen and empirical intravenous antibiotics regardless of how well or unwell they look, because clinical assessment poorly discriminates serious bacterial infection under 3 months. RCH recommends lumbar puncture with cefotaxime plus ampicillin/amoxicillin (for Listeria) plus aciclovir until herpes simplex encephalitis is excluded. Waiting for biomarkers to trend or discharging on oral antibiotics both risk missing bacterial meningitis or bacteraemia. This pathway is stricter than that used in older children where a source-driven approach is acceptable.
key_points: Fever under 3 months: full septic screen including lumbar puncture where safe.
Empirical cover: IV cefotaxime plus amoxicillin plus aciclovir until herpes simplex encephalitis excluded.
Clinical wellness and normal C reactive protein do not exclude serious bacterial infection in this age.
explanation.pearls: A 6 week old with a documented temperature of 38.4 degC gets lumbar puncture plus IV cefotaxime, amoxicillin and aciclovir even if he brightens briefly on the parent's lap.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Febrile child
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Sepsis in neonates and infants

subtopic_detail: Croup severity based dexamethasone dose per RCH
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar on evening shift. A 2 year old boy presents with a barking cough for 8 hours and stridor. He has no drooling, is tolerating small sips and is not toxic. His mother reports similar symptoms 6 months ago that settled with a single oral dexamethasone dose from a regional emergency department. He has no allergies and is fully vaccinated. There is no foreign body history. On examination he has occasional inspiratory stridor when upset but no stridor at rest, mild suprasternal recession only when crying, and normal air entry bilaterally.

He becomes calmer sitting on his father's lap. The bedside nurse asks what dexamethasone dose to draw up before you review him again in 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 130 /min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 /min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 37.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Inspiratory stridor only when upset, mild suprasternal recession when crying, no stridor at rest, tolerating oral fluids
data_table.Investigations: Not indicated; no chest X ray required in typical croup

lead_in: What is the most appropriate corticosteroid dose now?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg single dose now, review at 30 minutes and discharge if he remains clinically stable
options.rationale: Prednisolone is used in some services but dexamethasone is preferred for its longer half life and lower recurrence of symptoms in the following 24 hours; RCH lists dexamethasone first line. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised budesonide 2 mg as a single dose today with no additional oral steroid required at this visit
options.rationale: Nebulised budesonide is a second line option when oral dexamethasone is not tolerated; oral dexamethasone is preferred as first line where available. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 now, observe for 3 hours, no oral steroid required at this visit
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline is reserved for moderate to severe croup with stridor at rest; steroid should be given in mild and moderate cases and this child qualifies for oral dexamethasone. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg single dose now, arrange urgent retrieval to a tertiary paediatric intensive care unit
options.rationale: 0.6 mg/kg is only indicated for severe croup with stridor at rest and increased work of breathing; this child is mild with stridor only when upset and does not need tertiary retrieval. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

options.text: Oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose now, observe for 30 minutes then discharge home with croup advice
options.rationale: Mild and moderate croup are treated with oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg as a single dose; escalate to 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup with stridor at rest. Observation for 30 minutes is standard before discharge if he remains well. (Source: RCH CPG: Croup)

explanation.summary: RCH advises oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg for mild and moderate croup as a single dose, escalating to 0.6 mg/kg only for severe croup with stridor at rest, respiratory distress or agitation. Nebulised adrenaline is added for moderate to severe cases and needs 3 hours minimum observation after the last nebule. The disconfirming finding here is that the stridor is only present when upset and the child settles on his father's lap, which places him in the mild category and rules out the higher dose. Prednisolone is a fallback where dexamethasone is unavailable.
key_points: Mild/moderate croup: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg single dose.
Severe croup with stridor at rest: 0.6 mg/kg plus nebulised adrenaline 5 mL 1:1000, observe 3 hours.
Nebulised budesonide is a fallback when oral steroid cannot be given.
explanation.pearls: Stridor only when upset with normal air entry and no recession at rest is mild croup; give 0.15 mg/kg oral dexamethasone, not 0.6 mg/kg.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Croup
Therapeutic Guidelines Respiratory: Croup

subtopic_detail: ASCIA banded adrenaline dose for paediatric anaphylaxis
stem:
You are the emergency medicine registrar on a Sunday afternoon at a suburban emergency department. A 4 year old boy who weighs 16 kg presents 20 minutes after eating a peanut biscuit at a birthday party. He has widespread urticaria, facial swelling, harsh stridor at rest and vomiting. His mother reports mild wheeze at home which is now worse. He has a documented previous mild peanut reaction and carries no adrenaline autoinjector. He is placed supine with legs elevated because he is pale and tachycardic.

An ASCIA action plan is on the ward wall. The intern preparing the drug asks whether to use 10 microg/kg by weight, or the ASCIA banded intramuscular dose. Your consultant emphasises the AU standard. He has no known intercurrent medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 156 /min, blood pressure 78/50 mmHg, respiratory rate 40 /min, SpO2 92% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Urticaria over the trunk, facial and periorbital swelling, stridor at rest, wheeze, pale, capillary refill 3 s
data_table.Investigations: Not required at this point; peak flow deferred

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first dose of intramuscular adrenaline?

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 150 microg into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeat at 5 minutes if no response
options.rationale: ASCIA uses a banded weight table with 150 microg (0.15 mL 1:1000) for children 10 to 20 kg, given intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeatable every 5 minutes as required. This is the AU standard rather than the 10 microg/kg arithmetic approach. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 300 microg into the mid anterolateral thigh, repeat every 5 minutes
options.rationale: 300 microg (EpiPen dose) is the banded dose for children 20 kg and over; this child is 16 kg and falls into the 10 to 20 kg band, so the 150 microg dose is correct. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Intramuscular adrenaline 10 microg/kg = 160 microg via 1:10,000 preparation into the deltoid
options.rationale: 10 microg/kg arithmetic is not the AU banded standard, the 1:10,000 preparation is for intravenous or intraosseous rescue only, and the deltoid site is inferior to the anterolateral thigh in emergency doses. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microg/kg/min immediately without an intramuscular dose
options.rationale: Intravenous adrenaline infusion is reserved for refractory anaphylaxis after intramuscular doses have failed, given in a monitored high dependency or paediatric intensive care setting. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

options.text: Nebulised adrenaline 5 mL of 1:1000 plus intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg as first line
options.rationale: Nebulised adrenaline treats upper airway oedema symptomatically but is not a substitute for intramuscular adrenaline in anaphylaxis; hydrocortisone is second line and not the first drug. (Source: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis)
source_refs: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis

explanation.summary: ASCIA anaphylaxis guidelines use a banded weight table for intramuscular adrenaline: 150 microg for children 10 to 20 kg (equivalent to an EpiPen Junior), 300 microg for 20 kg and over, and 500 microg for large adolescents and adults. Doses are drawn from 1:1000 ampoule (or delivered by autoinjector) and given into the mid anterolateral thigh. Repeat every 5 minutes if the patient has not improved. 1:10,000 adrenaline is reserved for intravenous or intraosseous rescue and 10 microg/kg arithmetic is not the AU standard because banded dosing is faster and safer under stress.
key_points: ASCIA banded intramuscular adrenaline: 10 to 20 kg = 150 microg; 20 kg and over = 300 microg.
Intramuscular route into anterolateral thigh; repeat every 5 minutes.
1:10,000 preparation is for intravenous or intraosseous administration only, not intramuscular.
explanation.pearls: A 16 kg child in anaphylaxis gets 150 microg (0.15 mL of 1:1000) intramuscularly into the mid anterolateral thigh - the banded ASCIA dose, not 10 microg/kg arithmetic.

sources.label: ASCIA Guidelines for Acute Management of Anaphylaxis
RCH CPG: Anaphylaxis

subtopic_detail: Refractory paediatric septic shock with severe hypokalaemia after fluid resuscitation
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional emergency department awaiting retrieval to the tertiary paediatric intensive care unit. A 3 year old boy weighing 15 kg presents with 24 hours of fever, vomiting and lethargy. Meningococcal petechial rash appeared 30 minutes before arrival. He has had appropriate IV access, blood cultures, IV ceftriaxone 100 mg/kg within the first hour, and 60 mL/kg 0.9 percent saline in 20 mL/kg aliquots over 45 minutes. He is now less mottled but blood pressure remains low with a widened pulse pressure.

He has been placed on peripheral inotrope by protocol (adrenaline 0.1 microg/kg/min) as central line placement is in progress. Repeat blood gas after the third bolus shows severe hypokalaemia. Urine has been passed once (1 mL/kg/hour). He is not producing arrhythmia yet on cardiac monitor. Retrieval team arrives in 30 minutes.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 74/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 96% on 4 L via nasal prongs, temperature 39.1 degC
data_table.Examination: Alert but quiet, purpuric rash spreading, capillary refill 3 s post fluids, no dysrhythmia on monitor
data_table.Investigations: pH 7.22, HCO3 14 mmol/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, potassium 2.4 mmol/L, chloride 112 mmol/L, ionised calcium 1.05 mmol/L, glucose 5.6 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step now, prior to retrieval?

options.text: Deliver a fourth 20 mL/kg saline bolus now and escalate adrenaline to 0.3 microg/kg/min while searching for the cause of the acute hypokalaemia
options.rationale: Further crystalloid beyond 60 mL/kg without addressing severe hypokalaemia risks hyperchloraemic acidosis and pulmonary oedema and does not treat the arrhythmogenic potassium; further volume before correcting potassium is not the appropriate step. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Commence a peripheral potassium infusion at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour via a large bore line with continuous cardiac monitoring, continue current adrenaline
options.rationale: Severe hypokalaemia at 2.4 mmol/L in a shocked child is arrhythmogenic and precipitates cardiac arrest particularly during catecholamine therapy; the correct step is to begin controlled potassium replacement at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour under continuous monitoring while maintaining current inotropic support until central access allows noradrenaline. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Bolus intravenous potassium chloride 20 mmol over 15 minutes to correct the potassium rapidly, then reassess perfusion and any further vasopressor requirement
options.rationale: Rapid potassium bolus is contraindicated because of high arrhythmia risk; the recommended rate is 0.5 mmol/kg/hour via continuous infusion with cardiac monitoring, not a bolus. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Commence intravenous hydrocortisone 2 mg/kg for suspected relative adrenal insufficiency prior to inotrope escalation and defer potassium replacement
options.rationale: Hydrocortisone is reasonable in catecholamine resistant shock but is not the pre eminent step here; ignoring an arrhythmogenic potassium of 2.4 mmol/L exposes the child to sudden arrest and it should be corrected in parallel or ahead of steroid consideration. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

options.text: Intubate and ventilate now then commence renal replacement therapy for lactic acidosis correction prior to retrieval by the paediatric intensive care team
options.rationale: Intubation and renal replacement are not indicated at present given adequate oxygenation and moderate lactate; both delay the immediate correction of the arrhythmogenic hypokalaemia and could precipitate arrest during induction. (Source: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis)

explanation.summary: A shocked 3 year old with a potassium of 2.4 mmol/L is at high risk of arrhythmia and arrest, particularly under catecholamine infusion. The Australian paediatric sepsis pathway prioritises antibiotics within the hour, up to 60 mL/kg fluid in aliquots and early vasopressor via peripheral or intraosseous route; once refractory, the next competing priorities are correcting severe electrolyte disturbance and moving from peripheral adrenaline to noradrenaline via central access. Rapid potassium bolus is unsafe; instead a monitored infusion of 0.5 mmol/kg/hour balances speed and safety. Steroid, ventilation and renal replacement each have narrower roles and do not address the immediate arrhythmia risk.
key_points: Severe hypokalaemia in septic shock is arrhythmogenic and must be corrected by infusion, not bolus.
Standard paediatric potassium replacement is up to 0.5 mmol/kg/hour with continuous cardiac monitoring.
Central noradrenaline is preferred to escalating peripheral adrenaline once catecholamine resistance emerges.
explanation.pearls: In a shocked child with potassium 2.4 mmol/L, run a monitored potassium infusion at 0.5 mmol/kg/hour and prepare to switch to central noradrenaline; do not bolus potassium or push more crystalloid.

sources.label: ANZCOR paediatric sepsis
RCH CPG: Sepsis
Surviving Sepsis Campaign International Guidelines for Paediatric Sepsis and Septic Shock

subtopic_detail: Neonate with duct dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease refractory to prostaglandin E1
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a regional level 2 nursery. A 3 day old term neonate is transferred from the postnatal ward with sudden cyanosis feeding. Antenatal ultrasound was reported as normal. Oxygen saturation is 68% right hand and 62% right foot. She was placed on prostaglandin E1 at 0.05 microg/kg/min after venous access 20 minutes ago in liaison with a paediatric cardiology fellow on retrieval line, presuming a duct dependent cyanotic congenital heart disease. Saturations have not improved after 20 minutes at 0.1 microg/kg/min.

She is now on 100 percent oxygen through a headbox with no rise in saturations. Echocardiogram over telehealth by the cardiologist shows d-transposition of the great arteries with an intact ventricular septum and a restrictive atrial communication. The retrieval team is 90 minutes away.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 168 /min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg, respiratory rate 66 /min, SpO2 62% preductal, temperature 36.6 degC
data_table.Examination: Central cyanosis, tachypnoea, no murmur, hepatomegaly absent, femoral pulses palpable equally
data_table.Investigations: Point of care echocardiogram (via telehealth) d-transposition of the great arteries, intact ventricular septum, restrictive foramen ovale, patent ductus arteriosus small, no other lesion

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step to improve oxygenation before retrieval?

options.text: Increase prostaglandin E1 to 0.4 microg/kg/min and add inhaled nitric oxide at 20 parts per million to improve pulmonary flow
options.rationale: In d-transposition with a restrictive atrial septum, further ductal opening does not improve mixing because the systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel; nitric oxide can worsen the mismatch. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Cease prostaglandin E1 infusion, commence dobutamine 10 microg/kg/min and pack the neonate in ice to reduce cerebral oxygen demand
options.rationale: Cessation of prostaglandin E1 removes a small source of mixing at the duct; inotrope alone does not treat the parallel circulation and induced hypothermia is not the immediate step for a duct dependent lesion. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Bedside balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) under echocardiographic guidance to allow atrial level mixing while awaiting retrieval
options.rationale: In d-transposition of the great arteries with an intact ventricular septum and restrictive atrial communication, cyanosis is due to inadequate mixing at atrial level; a balloon atrial septostomy performed under echocardiographic guidance improves mixing and is a temporising manoeuvre before the arterial switch. Prostaglandin alone is insufficient when the atrial septum is restrictive. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Emergency intubation with hyperventilation to a pCO2 of 25 mmHg and permissive hyperoxia to drive pulmonary vasodilatation
options.rationale: Hyperventilation and hyperoxia in a parallel circulation do not increase mixing and can be harmful; the driver of hypoxia here is inadequate atrial mixing not pulmonary vascular resistance. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

options.text: Commence extracorporeal membrane oxygenation via a peripheral cannula in the regional nursery before retrieval by the tertiary team
options.rationale: Extracorporeal membrane oxygenation is not a peripheral bedside procedure in a regional nursery and does not address the anatomical problem; balloon atrial septostomy under echocardiographic guidance is the standard temporising step. (Source: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook)
source_refs: ANZ Paediatric and Neonatal Cardiology handbook

explanation.summary: d-transposition of the great arteries places the pulmonary and systemic circulations in parallel; adequate mixing depends on the atrial septum, ventricular septum or ductus arteriosus. When the ventricular septum is intact and the atrial communication is restrictive, oxygenation cannot improve with prostaglandin E1 alone because there is minimal ductal mixing available. Emergency balloon atrial septostomy (Rashkind procedure) under echocardiographic guidance enlarges the interatrial communication, increases mixing and buys time for the arterial switch operation. Prostaglandin continues but is not the answer to persistent cyanosis in this specific anatomy.
key_points: d-transposition: systemic and pulmonary circulations run in parallel; oxygenation depends on mixing.
Restrictive atrial communication in d-transposition demands balloon atrial septostomy, not more prostaglandin.
Arterial switch is the surgical goal; septostomy is the temporising manoeuvre.
explanation.pearls: For d-transposition of the great arteries with intact ventricular septum and restrictive atrial communication and persistent cyanosis on prostaglandin E1, the temporising manoeuvre is a balloon atrial septostomy.

subtopic_detail: Vaginal birth after caesarean eligibility criteria per RANZCOG
stem:
You are the obstetrics and gynaecology registrar in a district hospital antenatal clinic. A 33 year old woman is 36 weeks pregnant with an uncomplicated singleton pregnancy in cephalic presentation. Her first birth was 3 years ago by lower segment caesarean for breech at term with a low transverse incision documented in the operative report. She had no wound complications and her postnatal recovery was uncomplicated. This pregnancy has been uneventful with normal glucose tolerance test, normal blood pressure, normal ultrasound growth, and a normally sited placenta anteriorly not overlying the previous scar.

She is keen to plan a vaginal birth this time and asks about eligibility. The birth suite is midwife led with an on site obstetric registrar 24 hours, a general theatre with 30 minute recall for elective work, and continuous cardiotocograph monitoring available. Anaesthetics can be on site within 15 minutes overnight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 82 /min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degC
data_table.Examination: Symphysial fundal height 35 cm, cephalic, longitudinal lie, foetal heart 142 /min, no palpable contractions
data_table.Investigations: Foetal ultrasound 34 weeks estimated foetal weight 55th centile, placenta anterior high, cervix long closed

lead_in: Which single feature makes planned vaginal birth after caesarean in this hospital inappropriate?

options.text: The indication for her previous caesarean was breech presentation at term with a low transverse uterine scar
options.rationale: The indication for the previous caesarean does not itself preclude a planned vaginal birth after caesarean; a low transverse scar with a resolved non recurring indication is a good candidate. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: The inter delivery interval since the previous caesarean is 3 years with no complications during that time
options.rationale: An inter delivery interval of 18 to 24 months and above is considered acceptable; 3 years does not preclude a planned vaginal birth. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: The current pregnancy is at 36 weeks with a cephalic singleton and normal foetal growth on scan
options.rationale: 36 weeks is not a preclusive gestation; term vaginal birth after caesarean is standard. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: Anaesthetics and theatre availability with a 30 minute recall for elective work rather than immediate in house response
options.rationale: RANZCOG requires the ability to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of a decision, meaning immediate access to anaesthetics and theatre for uterine rupture. A 30 minute recall for elective theatre with 15 minute anaesthetic on call overnight does not meet that immediate response requirement and makes planned vaginal birth after caesarean inappropriate at this facility. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

options.text: The anteriorly located placenta is not overlying the previous caesarean scar on the recent morphology scan
options.rationale: An anterior placenta not overlying the scar and normally sited does not preclude planned vaginal birth after caesarean; placenta accreta risk with anterior placenta over the scar would. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean

explanation.summary: Planned vaginal birth after caesarean requires a low transverse uterine scar, a resolved or non recurring indication, appropriate inter delivery interval, continuous cardiotocograph monitoring and immediate access to obstetric, anaesthetic and theatre teams to perform emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of the decision. Facility rather than obstetric factors are the reason planned vaginal birth after caesarean is declined here. Anterior placenta not overlying the scar is safe; anterior placenta overlying the previous caesarean scar prompts placenta accreta workup. Inter delivery interval and previous indication are not disqualifying in this scenario.
key_points: Emergency caesarean within 30 minutes of decision is a RANZCOG facility requirement for vaginal birth after caesarean.
Low transverse scar with resolved indication is a favourable feature.
Anterior placenta over the scar (not off the scar) prompts placenta accreta workup.
explanation.pearls: A 30 minute theatre recall for elective work is not the immediate response needed for uterine rupture; refer to a facility with in house theatre for planned vaginal birth after caesarean.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 38 Planned Vaginal Birth After Caesarean
NSW Health Maternity - vaginal birth after caesarean

subtopic_detail: Group B streptococcus intrapartum antibiotic choice in a woman with severe penicillin allergy
stem:
You are the obstetrics registrar reviewing a 29 year old primigravida in early labour at 39 weeks gestation. She had a vaginal group B streptococcus swab at 36 weeks that was positive. She has a documented severe penicillin allergy (immediate anaphylaxis with tongue swelling and hypotension after an intramuscular procaine penicillin dose as a teenager). Her group B streptococcus isolate has been sensitivity tested and is reported as susceptible to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin (inducible resistance detected on D test), and sensitivity to vancomycin not requested by the laboratory.

She is contracting every 5 minutes with intact membranes. The birth suite midwife asks for the antibiotic order to give now. There is no other allergy and no other medical comorbidity. She has had no doses of prophylaxis yet.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92 /min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 /min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degC
data_table.Examination: Cervix 3 cm dilated, intact membranes, cephalic, foetal heart 138 /min
data_table.Investigations: GBS swab positive; sensitivities susceptible to penicillin, resistant to clindamycin with D test inducible resistance, no vancomycin sensitivity reported

lead_in: Which intrapartum antibiotic regimen is most appropriate?

options.text: Intravenous benzylpenicillin 3 g loading dose then 1.8 g every 4 hours until delivery, no allergy modification needed
options.rationale: Benzylpenicillin is contraindicated because of her documented immediate anaphylaxis to penicillin. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous cefazolin 2 g loading dose then 1 g every 8 hours until delivery via a peripheral cannula in this labour
options.rationale: Cephalosporins share a small cross reactivity with penicillins and are relatively contraindicated when the reaction was immediate anaphylaxis; select an alternative not sharing the beta lactam core. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous clindamycin 900 mg every 8 hours until delivery via a peripheral cannula throughout this labour period
options.rationale: The isolate is resistant to clindamycin with D test inducible resistance; clindamycin cannot be relied on for group B streptococcus prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Oral erythromycin 500 mg every 6 hours starting now and continued until delivery of the infant in this labour
options.rationale: Erythromycin has variable resistance in group B streptococcus and poor placental transfer; it is not recommended as intrapartum prophylaxis. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

options.text: Intravenous vancomycin 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours over at least 60 minutes until delivery, per AU guidance
options.rationale: With immediate penicillin anaphylaxis and clindamycin resistance on D test, vancomycin is the recommended prophylaxis at 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours infused over at least 60 minutes until delivery. Sensitivity to vancomycin does not need to be reported for empiric intrapartum use. (Source: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy

explanation.summary: The Australasian intrapartum prophylaxis pathway for group B streptococcus uses benzylpenicillin as first line; a woman with immediate hypersensitivity to penicillin has cephalosporins relatively contraindicated. Clindamycin may be used only when the isolate is sensitive and no inducible resistance is detected on D test; where either is unavailable or resistance is present, vancomycin is the recommended alternative. Erythromycin is no longer routinely recommended. Vancomycin is dosed at 20 mg/kg (maximum 2 g) every 8 hours infused over at least 60 minutes to reduce infusion related hypersensitivity. Adequate prophylaxis is at least one dose 4 hours before birth.
key_points: Benzylpenicillin is first line; anaphylaxis is a hard contraindication.
Clindamycin requires proven susceptibility and no inducible resistance on D test.
Vancomycin is the fallback where clindamycin cannot be used, 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours over 60 minutes.
explanation.pearls: In severe penicillin anaphylaxis with clindamycin resistance, intrapartum group B streptococcus prophylaxis is vancomycin 20 mg/kg (max 2 g) every 8 hours over at least 60 minutes.

sources.label: RANZCOG Statement C-Obs 19 Maternal group B streptococcus in pregnancy
Therapeutic Guidelines Antibiotic: Group B streptococcus prophylaxis
